headline: Genetic tests are changing families in two ways

sources.title: The power of genetic testing: new screening methods are catching rare diseases before symptoms start (CNBC)
The DNA discovery boom: How at-home tests are rewriting American family trees (Stacker, via KRDO)
When DNA tests find skeletons in your family's closet, these researchers want to know about it (Religion News Service)

chunks.text: At-home DNA tests are a common gift in the United States. By March 2026, the three biggest companies held more than 54 million [[test kits]], a news report said on August 25. Millions of customers {{sign up}} to learn about their [[ancestry]]. But many {{find out}} something else. In a 2025 [[survey]], one in four tested Americans said unknown [[close relatives]] {{turned up}} in their results.

verbs.correct: To agree to join or use a service
verbs.wrong: To give official approval to a plan
verbs.why: You can sign up for a gym class online in two minutes. She signed up for a cooking course last spring. Millions of customers sign up for DNA tests just to learn about their ancestry.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To complete a form with your details
verbs.why: I found out that my flight was canceled only at the airport. He wants to find out who sent the letter. Many customers find out about unknown relatives when their DNA results arrive.

verbs.correct: To appear when nobody expected it
verbs.why: My lost keys turned up in the freezer. An old photo turned up during the move. In one survey, one in four tested Americans said unknown close relatives turned up in their results.

chunks.text: A 2022 study of 23,000 test customers found that 82 percent had discovered at least one unknown [[genetic relative]]. About 3 percent learned a parent {{turned out}} not to be their [[biological parent]]. When people {{reached out}} to new [[siblings]], 92 percent of those siblings {{got back to}} them. Three in four called the [[outcome]] positive or neutral, although some needed time to {{take in}} the news.

verbs.correct: To be found to be true at the end
verbs.why: The cheap hotel turned out to be the best part of the trip. The rumor turned out to be false. For about 3 percent of people in the study, a parent turned out not to be their biological parent.

verbs.correct: To make contact with someone new
verbs.wrong: To take back something you said
verbs.why: A recruiter reached out to me on a job site last week. She reached out to a neighbor she had never met. In the study, people reached out to new siblings, and most of the siblings answered.

verbs.correct: To reply to someone who contacted you
verbs.wrong: To return an item to a store
verbs.why: I will get back to you by Friday with an answer. The landlord never got back to us about the leak. In the study, 92 percent of newly found siblings got back to the person who contacted them.

verbs.wrong: To tell other people some news
verbs.why: It took me a minute to take in the news about the layoffs. She sat down to take in what the doctor had said. Some people needed time to take in the news about a new relative.

chunks.text: Medical tests are changing families too. A Columbia University study in New York offers free [[genome]] sequencing to newborns, a business news channel reported on August 10. Standard [[newborn screening]] checks for 30 to 50 diseases; the study checks for 450. In the first 4,000 babies, the test {{picked up}} [[serious conditions]] in just under 4 percent. One baby girl received a [[diagnosis]] of a [[fatal]] nerve disease at six months, years before [[symptoms]] would {{show up}}. Doctors started a [[treatment]] that may {{hold off}} the [[damage]].

verbs.correct: To detect a problem or disease
verbs.wrong: To send a sample to a laboratory
verbs.why: A routine blood test picked up her low iron. The scanner picked up a small crack in the pipe. In the New York study, the genome test picked up serious conditions in just under 4 percent of babies.

verbs.wrong: To draw attention to a mistake
verbs.why: The rash showed up two days after the hike. Stress often shows up as trouble sleeping. The baby girl was diagnosed years before any symptoms would show up.

verbs.wrong: To repeat a test to be certain
verbs.why: The city hopes the new wall will hold off the floods. A vaccine can hold off the worst of the illness. Her doctors started a treatment that may hold off the nerve damage.

chunks.text: Researchers now ask what these discoveries do to families. In September 2026, a Brigham Young University historian and a DNA education company founder {{put out}} a call for [[personal stories]] on a new website, a news service reported on the 18th. They hope people will {{open up}} about how a DNA result changed their sense of family, or even their [[faith]]. Many will need to {{work through}} [[hard feelings]] first. Shared [[patterns]], they say, could help newcomers feel less alone.

verbs.correct: To make a request known to everyone
verbs.wrong: To cancel a project at the last minute
verbs.why: The police put out a call for witnesses after the crash. The theater put out a request for volunteers. In September, two researchers put out a call for personal stories about DNA discoveries.

verbs.correct: To talk freely about private feelings
verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: He finally opened up about his father's illness. It took months before she would open up to the counselor. The researchers hope people will open up about how a DNA result changed their family.

verbs.correct: To deal with a problem step by step
verbs.wrong: To leave a job without notice
verbs.why: The couple worked through their money problems with a counselor. It took him a year to work through his grief. Many participants will need to work through hard feelings about their DNA results.

mainIdea.s: Home DNA kits are revealing unknown relatives to many Americans, while a hospital study finds rare diseases in babies before symptoms. Researchers now want to learn how such results change families.
mainIdea.why: One in four tested Americans found unknown close relatives, a newborn genome test picked up serious conditions early, and two researchers put out a call for family stories.

mainIdea.s: Home DNA kits can now warn parents about rare diseases in their babies before any symptoms appear. Doctors say these cheap kits catch far more conditions than the screening done in hospitals.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the newborn results come from a free hospital study at Columbia University, not from at-home kits, which people buy to learn about ancestry and relatives.

mainIdea.s: A large DNA testing company has sold its customer database to a drug maker after going bankrupt. Millions of families now want to know what will happen to their private genetic information.
mainIdea.why: Nothing here describes a sale of customer data or a bankruptcy. The two developments are unexpected relatives from home kits and early diagnoses for newborns.

tf.s: One in four tested Americans said unknown close relatives turned up in their results.
tf.why: A 2025 survey found that one in four Americans who took a DNA test discovered close relatives they had never known about.

tf.s: Standard newborn screening picked up serious conditions in almost 4 percent of babies.
tf.why: The Columbia University genome test picked up serious conditions in just under 4 percent. Standard screening checks for far fewer diseases.

tf.s: When people reached out to new siblings, 92 percent of the siblings got back to them.
tf.why: In the 2022 study, newly found siblings answered 92 percent of the time when someone contacted them.

tf.s: Three in four people said the outcome of their DNA discovery was negative.
tf.why: Three in four called the outcome positive or neutral, even if some needed time to take in the news.

tf.s: The baby girl's diagnosis came only after her symptoms showed up.
tf.why: She was diagnosed at six months, years before any symptoms would show up, so her doctors could start a treatment that may hold off the damage.

tf.s: In September, researchers put out a call for personal stories on a new website.
tf.why: A university historian and a DNA company founder want people to open up about how a DNA result changed their sense of family.

lines.text: My cousin got a DNA kit for her birthday, and now she has a half brother in Ohio. Nobody in the family knew.
That happens more than you'd think. One in four Americans who take those tests say unknown close relatives {{turned up}}.
One in four? I thought people just {{signed up}} to see if they were part Irish.
Most do. Then they {{find out}} something else. In one study of 23,000 customers, 3 percent learned that a parent {{turned out}} not to be their biological parent.
[[You can't unknow that]]. What do people do with it?
Many {{reach out}}. And new siblings usually answer. In that study, 92 percent of them {{got back to}} the person who wrote.
Still, that's [[a lot to sit with]]. How did people feel afterward?
Three in four said it was positive or neutral. It just took some of them a while to {{take in}} the news.
The medical side is the part I care about. Did you read about the newborn study in New York?
The genome test? They screened 4,000 babies and {{picked up}} serious conditions in almost 4 percent. Standard screening checks for far fewer diseases.
And the baby girl with the nerve disease got her diagnosis at six months, before any symptoms {{showed up}}.
Right. So her doctors could start a treatment that might {{hold off}} the damage. With a disease like that, [[every day counts]].
I'd want to know, even if the answer was bad. [[Knowledge is power]]. My grandmother had a heart problem, and [[it runs in the family]].
Same here. And now two researchers have {{put out}} a call for stories from people whose results changed their sense of family.
So people can {{open up}} about it, even the messy parts. That seems healthy.
That's the idea. Most of us would need help to {{work through}} something like that.

expressions.def: Used to say that once a person learns a fact, they cannot go back to not knowing it
ex: He read his sister's diary. You can't unknow that.
I saw the kitchen at that restaurant. You can't unknow that.

expressions.def: Used about news that takes time to accept and think about
ex: A diagnosis like that is a lot to sit with.
Losing the house was a lot to sit with for the whole family.

expressions.def: Used to say that acting early matters because each day of delay does harm
ex: With a stroke, every day counts, so call the doctor now.
The harvest is late and every day counts.

expressions.def: Used to say that knowing the facts helps you make better choices
ex: Read the contract before you sign. Knowledge is power.
She checks her blood pressure every week. Knowledge is power.

expressions.def: Used to say that a trait or illness is shared by many relatives
ex: Both my parents have gray hair early. It runs in the family.
Diabetes runs in the family, so she gets checked every year.
